title: Think More or Read More? A Token-Budget Theory of Reasoning with Shared Context

paper.title: Think More or Read More? A Token-Budget Theory of Reasoning with Shared Context
paper.abstract:
Abstract Reasoning systems increasingly improve answers by incorporating additional context into the model’s input, from multi-agent debate, where agents read their peers’ responses, to self-refinement, where a model revisits its own drafts. In these systems, communication consumes context as one agent’s output becomes another’s input.
We study the regime where token reading and generation draw on one fixed token window, so every token spent reading is a token that cannot be spent reasoning.
We develop a token-budget theory that formalizes this trade-off, modeling accuracy as a function of the reasoning budget remaining after reading and aggregating votes with a Condorcet jury model that permits correlated errors.
For multi-agent debate, the theory gives a closed-form prediction for the optimal number of agents. This quantity is estimated from single-agent measurements, allowing the optimal group size to be determined without running debate, and the same accounting extends to a heterogeneous set of different models.
We empirically verify our theory and show that, at the predicted group size, our method outperforms strong baselines under the tightest calibration spend, where debate-calibrated rules can afford only one or two questions.
Self-refinement obeys the same accounting, with its own draft in place of a peer message.
The theory further predicts that communication pays only when the gain in the accuracy ceiling exceeds the reasoning room spent on reading, with this condition tightening as the window shrinks.
Across five open models and four reasoning tasks, self-consistency matches or beats deployed debate at 93 93 % of 980 980 matched window-and-group-size settings, with the gap being largest under tight windows and nearly disappearing at a loose one, consistent with the theory.
Under a shared window, how much room a model has left to think matters more than what it reads .

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in reasoning pipelines that reuse model-generated text as input to subsequent computation. Multi-agent debate exchanges answers among agents ( Du et al., 2024 ; Liang et al., 2024 ) , while self-refinement feeds a model its own previous drafts ( Madaan et al., 2023 ) . Such reuse can improve reasoning by providing additional information, but under a fixed token budget, it also raises a fundamental question: not whether added feedback helps, but how much it is worth in terms of the reasoning budget it consumes. Figure 1: Overview of our method (Qwen2.5-7B, GSM8K). One window W W pays for both reading (question plus peer messages) and thinking (generation g g ), and each extra agent adds m m tokens of reading. The per-agent edge δ \delta is the gap between the probability of the correct answer and that of the strongest wrong answer: larger δ \delta means a stronger correct-answer margin, while δ ≤ 0 \delta\leq 0 means that a wrong answer is at least as likely. Left : The dashed line marks the smallest thinking room at which δ > 0 \delta>0 ; a group that reads past it (here n = 8 n{=}8 ) leaves too few tokens for reasoning and its accuracy collapses. Right : The effective sample size n eff n_{\mathrm{eff}} measures the independent-vote equivalent of n n correlated agents, while δ \delta falls as thinking room shrinks. Their product S S , the synergy index, therefore captures the trade-off between per-agent accuracy and voting amplification and peaks at n ∗ = 4.9 n^{\ast}=4.9 . The shaded band marks δ ≤ 0 \delta{\leq}0 , where votes amplify a wrong majority and extra agents cannot help. Majority-voting analyses predict that adding agents amplifies a correct majority until correlated errors cap the gain ( Ladha, 1992 ; Liu et al., 2026 ) . However, on multi-hop reasoning tasks, a single long chain-of-thought ( Wei et al., 2022 ) often matches or outperforms a multi-agent system under an equal thinking budget ( Tran and Kiela, 2026 ) . Debate also does not consistently outperform self-consistency on an accuracy-per-token-cost frontier ( Smit et al., 2024 ; Bertalanic and Fortuna, 2026 ) , echoing the broader trade-off between token expenditure and accuracy in sampling and search ( Snell et al., 2025 ; Brown et al., 2024 ) . The token budget deserves separate attention because it corresponds directly to the cost incurred in practice. At current API prices, inference can range from cents to tens of dollars per million tokens, depending on the model and provider ( OpenAI, 2026 ; Google, 2026 ; Anthropic, 2026 ) . For multi-agent debate, the cost grows further with the number of agents n n (group size): adding agents increases not only the amount of reasoning generated, but also the amount of peer text that must be read and processed. Existing work attacks this cost either by compressing agent communication or by fixing the reasoning budget, but treats communication and reasoning as separate costs, despite both consuming the same token budget ( § \lx@sectionsign 2 ). Once the token budget is viewed this way, a trade-off appears: with n n small, more of the budget remains for thinking, while with n n large, most of it is spent on reading peer messages, leaving little room to reason. The question is then how to estimate the best group size n ∗ n^{\ast} for multi-agent debate under this trade-off. Existing approaches measure n n by sweeping or adaptively searching the design space, for instance, successive halving ( Jamieson and Talwalkar, 2016 ) . Both require debate runs to identify the operating point, without explaining why one group size is optimal or when adding more agents stops improving accuracy. We therefore introduce a token-budget theory that answers both questions in closed form. Consider homogeneous debate in which each agent, working under a window of W W tokens, must first pay for what it reads, namely the question and its peers’ messages, together H H tokens, plus a small fixed overhead c c . The remainder, g = W − H − c g=W-H-c , is the room it has left to reason. Instead of assigning each agent a fixed chance of voting correctly, we introduce its ability , which is the accuracy it reaches when its reasoning is capped at g g tokens. Ability grows with thinking room, too little room can prevent an agent from reaching an answer, while beyond a sufficient room, additional tokens yield little further gain. We let it grow with g g (Eq. 3 ) via the fittable thinking-gain function ϕ \phi , whose functional form and parameters can be calibrated from held-out calibration data. We then combine the resulting votes with a Condorcet jury model that allows correlated errors, developing the per-answer margin δ \delta (Eq. 6 ), the group accuracy A ⁡ ( n ) A(n) , the effective sample size n eff n_{\mathrm{eff}} and the synergy index S ⁡ ( n ) = δ ​ n eff S(n)=\delta\sqrt{n_{\mathrm{eff}}} (Eq. 10 ) in Section 3 . Figure 1 provides an overview of our method. Our model yields a closed-form prediction of an interior optimal group size n ∗ n^{\ast} that moves with the budget . It is read off single-agent measurements: we measure the ability curve with a cap sweep and estimate one error-correlation parameter at the initial round , then predict group size without running the debate. With a sufficiently large budget, our predictions approach the classical correlation-limited ensemble, where the main benefit comes from aggregating independent evidence. The practical advantage of our approach is therefore greatest in the tight-budget regime, where choosing the group size correctly matters most and our method achieves the best accuracy-budget trade-off. At the predicted size, it incurs only a 1.4 % 1.4\% accuracy gap from a per-cell oracle, using between 26 26 and 79 79 calibration questions depending on the cell, where the debate-calibrated rules use only one or two at matched spend. The accounting extends to a heterogeneous model set, where the rule chooses which models to include as well as how many. Our framework also clarifies the cost of communication relative to self-consistency ( Wang et al., 2023 ) . Self-consistency leaves the full window available for reasoning, whereas debate spends part of that budget processing peer responses, so communication must provide sufficient informational benefit to justify this cost. In our experiments, self-consistency matches or beats deployed debate at 93 % 93\% of the 980 980 matched operating points, while a paired test finds debate significantly ahead at only 0.5 % 0.5\% . The gap is largest under tight budgets and nearly disappears at a loose budget, where communication consumes a smaller share of the available reasoning budget. Self-refinement, which rereads only its own last draft without voting, pays the same fixed reading cost every round with none of the amplification that voting provides, so its accuracy collapses faster than debate’s as rounds accumulate. Our contributions are as follows. First , we introduce a token-budget theory that predicts the optimal debate size n ∗ n^{\ast} in closed form and extends to heterogeneous model sets, outperforming strong baselines under the tightest calibration spend without running a debate. Second , the theory reveals when debate’s voting benefits outweigh its communication cost relative to self-consistency under the same token budget. Third , ablations show that reading cost drives collapse and the interior optimum, with robustness tests covering longer reasoning and practical token pricing.

sections.heading: Multi-agent debate in LLMs.
sections.text: LLM instances critique and revise each other’s answers to improve reasoning relative to a single pass ( Du et al., 2024 ; Liang et al., 2024 ) , and voting over more agents can improve accuracy in practice ( Wang et al., 2023 ; Li et al., 2024a ) . Each additional agent, however, also introduces peer messages that other agents must process, increasing the communication burden of the group. Existing work addresses this burden by reducing communication through sparse speaker selection, group partitioning, or retaining only conflicting messages ( Li et al., 2024b ; Liu et al., 2024b ; Zeng et al., 2025 ; Nguyen et al., 2026c ) . A complementary line studies whether debate is worthwhile under a matched sampling or thinking budget, with several works finding that self-correction or a single long reasoning chain can match or outperform debate ( Huang et al., 2024 ; Tran and Kiela, 2026 ; Bertalanic and Fortuna, 2026 ) . A third line promotes diversity through heterogeneous model sets, arguing that homogeneous evaluation overvalues debate ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) , attributing vanilla debate’s weakness to lost candidate diversity ( Zhu et al., 2026 ) , and showing that mixed panels revise less harmfully than homogeneous ones ( Nilayam et al., 2026 ) . Beyond debate, this idea appears in mixtures of agents ( Wang et al., 2025 ) , model routing ( Ong et al., 2025 ) , and cost-aware cascades ( Chen et al., 2023 ) .

sections.heading: Estimating the operating point.
sections.text: Existing approaches search the design space, e.g., via successive halving ( Jamieson and Talwalkar, 2016 ) , or learn the operating point from data, but both require debate runs for calibration. Chen et al. (2024) make voting accuracy non-monotone in call count through query-difficulty diversity, but their optimum is refit separately at each budget, whereas ours transfers from a single-agent cap sweep. Liu et al. (2026) give the closest theoretical treatment, deriving an amplification-collapse threshold in closed form from a power-law ability curve. Their ability curve is calibrated in simulation and remains concave, so it cannot capture the near-zero accuracy below the minimum length needed for a solution, the regime where our collapse occurs. Their accounting also holds the per-agent generation allowance fixed, so adding an agent costs no reasoning room, making their collapse a consequence of correlation alone rather than reading. We recover their setting as the m = 0 m=0 case ( § \lx@sectionsign 4.3 ).

sections.heading: Token Budgeting in LLMs.
sections.text: A separate line studies how to allocate a fixed token budget across samples or reasoning length for a single agent, including token budgets for chain-of-thought, budget forcing at decoding time, budget-aligned tree search, and the non-monotone effect of reasoning length on task success ( Han et al., 2025 ; Muennighoff et al., 2025 ; Miyamoto et al., 2026 ; Qi, 2026 ) . Controlled comparisons at matched sampling or search budgets find that voting, rather than talking, carries the gain ( Choi et al., 2025 ; Kaesberg et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2024a ) , while Wunderlich et al. (2026) report the opposite ordering under per-agent rather than shared contexts. These methods budget within reasoning or sampling, leaving peer text outside the account.

sections.heading: 3 Method
sections.text: We formalize the token-budget problem behind debate, define per-agent ability as a function of the room left to think, and turn it into a group-accuracy prediction. We call the resulting predictor TB-MAD , for token-budget multi-agent debate: it reads a single-agent probe sweep and returns the group size, with no debate run.

sections.heading: 3.1 Problem Formulation
sections.text: Consider n n LLM agents that debate a question from a task Q Q over several rounds under one token budget W W , the window . Reading and thinking draw on the same W W , where tokens spent reading peer messages are tokens no longer available for the agent’s own chain of thought, and vice versa. Each peer message costs about m m tokens on average to read once. Under last-round visibility, which we use throughout, agent i i retains the question ( q q tokens), a fixed overhead ( c c ), and n − 1 n-1 peer messages, so its retained history and remaining room to think are H = q + ( n − 1 ) ​ m , g = W − H − c . \displaystyle H\;=\;q+(n-1)\,m,\qquad\qquad g\;=\;W-H-c. (1) Retaining the full transcript would increase H H at every n n and can only decrease g g , so the penalty we measure is a lower bound. Self-refinement uses a different accounting. The group size is one, so there are no peer messages, but the agent retains its own last draft. Its history is H = q + m H=q+m and its room is g = W − q − m − c g=W-q-m-c . In contrast, Eq. 1 with n = 1 n=1 describes a debate agent with no peer messages, corresponding to self-consistency. Adding an agent raises H H and lowers g g by m m tokens, which cuts both ways. When W W is generous, g g stays past the point where extra tokens stop buying accuracy and a larger group is close to free. When W W is tight, the agent pushes g g below the room a chain needs to reach an answer, and the lost generation budget outweighs the extra vote. We call this collapse : under a shared budget, more agents can reduce accuracy. Given W W , we want the group size that maximizes task accuracy, max n ⁡ A Q ​ ( n , W ) s.t. g ⁡ ( n ) = W − H ⁡ ( n ) − c ≥ 0 , \displaystyle\max_{n}\;A_{Q}(n,W)\quad\text{s.t.}\quad g(n)=W-H(n)-c\geq 0, (2) where A Q ​ ( n , W ) A_{Q}(n,W) is the debate group’s accuracy at size n n and window W W . Since a debate agent’s vote depends on how much of the window it got to reason in, solving Eq. 2 needs a model of per-agent ability as a function of g g , which we give next.

sections.heading: Models, Data And Metrics.
sections.text: We run five open instruction models across four families from 3 3 – 12 12 B: Llama-3.2-3B ( Llama Team, AI @ Meta, 2024 ) , Qwen2.5-7B ( Qwen Team, 2025 ) , Falcon3-7B ( Technology Innovation Institute, 2024 ) , Gemma-2-9B ( Gemma Team, 2024 ) and Gemma-3-12B ( Gemma Team, 2025 ) . We use four reasoning benchmarks, two difficulty levels in math and two non-math domains: GSM8K ( Cobbe et al., 2021 ) , MATH500 ( Lightman et al., 2024 ) , ten-way MMLU-Pro ( Wang et al., 2024b ) and five-way CSQA ( Talmor et al., 2019 ) (Appendix Table 3 ). For all tasks, we report accuracy in percentage.

sections.heading: Baselines.
sections.text: We compare our closed-form prediction against eight alternatives grouped by calibration cost. Debate-calibrated , using outcomes from actual debate runs that our method does not require: Empirical Argmax selects the best accuracy among tested ( n , W ) (n,W) configurations, Successive Halving ( Jamieson and Talwalkar, 2016 ) spends the same budget adaptively, and a Quadratic Surface in ( n , W ) (n,W) . No calibration: naive n = 1 n{=}1 and naive n = n max n{=}n_{\max} . Probe-calibrated, as ours is: Learned β eff \beta_{\mathrm{eff}} replaces the functional form with gradient-boosted trees; Star Exponent ( Liu et al., 2026 ) substitutes the power-law ability curve into our aggregator and budget model, which isolates the effect of the functional form; and Difficulty Mixture ( Chen et al., 2024 ) estimates per-question accuracy from probe sweeps and simulates voting, with the per-call allowance adjusted under our window accounting as n n varies. More details are in Appendix B.2 .

sections.text: We report regret as the percentage-point accuracy gap between the selected group size and an oracle that chooses the highest-accuracy configuration for each model–dataset pair. For all baselines, the first 40 % 40\% of test samples are used for calibration and the remaining 60 % 60\% for evaluation, with calibration costs accounted for as described in Appendix B.3 . All runs use vLLM ( Kwon et al., 2023 ) at temperature 1.0 1.0 across three seeds, pooling samples across seeds before fitting rather than fitting each seed separately and averaging the estimates. This choice has negligible effect on the results (Appendix B.1 ). More details are in Appendix B . sections.heading: Fitting And Predicting Performance.
sections.text: β eff ​ ( g ) \beta_{\mathrm{eff}}(g) is measured by capping one agent’s generation at g g , then fitting ( p max , g 0 , κ ) (p_{\max},g_{0},\kappa) , with the hill form chosen on held-out error from five candidate forms (Appendix Table 9 ). Using this fit, TB-MAD achieves the lowest regret, averaging 1.40 % 1.40\% and staying below 2 % 2\% across all models and eight comparisons at equal calibration spends (Table 2 ). The difference is largely driven by calibration cost: debate-calibrated rules afford far fewer questions, since debate expands input and output tokens by up to 49 × 49\times and 11 × 11\times (Appendix Table 11 ). Among probe-based methods, Star Exponent uses a power law that has higher held-out RMSE than the selected hill form (Appendix Table 9 ), while Difficulty Mixture estimates a per-question difficulty that is more data-hungry; Learned β eff \beta_{\mathrm{eff}} is the closest but trails while sacrificing interpretability. Actual n ∗ n^{*} predictions at 1 1 M spend are in Appendix Figure 7 . Broken out by window, TB-MAD is within 1 % 1\% of the best rule at six of the seven windows, trailing by 1.16 % 1.16\% at W = 2500 W{=}2500 (Appendix Table 20 ). Its performance is therefore not driven by a single region of the sweep.

sections.heading: TB-MAD Scaling Behavior.
sections.text: TB-MAD provides the best regret-cost trade-off, with regret decreasing as the calibration set grows (Figure 2 ). Its plain regret is already among the lowest at 10 10 calibration questions and stays roughly flat beyond 60 60 , since one probe-fitted ability curve gains little from more data. Debate-calibrated baselines start higher and keep dropping, closing part of that gap while their cost climbs (left panel). At equal spend, TB-MAD achieves the lowest regret and saturates once the maximum number of calibration questions is reached, whereas debate-based baselines keep improving as more tokens are spent, and Successive Halving overtakes TB-MAD at the largest budget.

sections.heading: Robustness to Heterogeneous Settings.
sections.text: We extend the evaluation to a heterogeneous setting with K K unique models, each appearing with the same model count, and isolate the allocation problem (Appendix C ). The probe-calibrated methods are again the strongest, and Learned β eff \beta_{\text{eff}} edges ahead of TB-MAD. Our rule trades a small amount of regret for a closed form and an explicit model-selection gate (Appendix Tables 12 and 13 ).

sections.heading: Generalization To Self-Refinement.
sections.text: Revision inherits the same generation-floor effect as debate, making self-refinement similarly token-inefficient: tight windows can reduce accuracy before any refinement benefit emerges. Useful refinement also requires both headroom and self-correction ability, so gains remain modest relative to the added token cost (Appendix D.1 ).

sections.heading: When More Agents Do Not Pay.
sections.text: Reading peers costs generation, which resolves two questions often studied separately. First, communication does not pay as majority voting with no communication matches or beats debate at 93 % 93\% of the 980 980 matched ( n , W ) (n,W) operating points with n ≥ 2 n\geq 2 (Appendix Table 18 ). A paired bootstrap on the same cells is more favourable still. Self-consistency is significantly better in 57 % 57\% of cases, debate in just 0.5 % 0.5\% , and the remaining 42.5 % 42.5\% are indistinguishable. The benefit of voting over debate has also been reported at matched sampling budgets ( Smit et al., 2024 ; Choi et al., 2025 ) . More importantly, Eq. 11 says when the ordering should reverse, and we test that prediction across seven windows rather than at a single operating point. At W = 1200 W{=}1200 , the margin is + 42.0 % +42.0\% , or + 13.7 % +13.7\% restricting to cells where g g is not clipped to the floor. It falls below 1 1 point by W = 6 ​ k W{=}6\mathrm{k} and is indistinguishable from zero through 32 ​ k 32\mathrm{k} on Qwen2.5-7B/GSM8K (Appendix Table 16 ), in line with Appendix Cor. 3 ’s correlation ceiling. The measured debate accuracy includes one revision round, so the observed margin also includes a revision lift not covered by Prop. 2 , estimated at 0.0 0.0 – 6.7 % 6.7\% (Table 14 , Appendix D.1 ). Second, a group is not always worth forming: a single agent matches or beats the debate group at 47 % 47\% of the 980 980 cells (Appendix Table 18 , single ≥ \geq group column), with δ > 0 \delta>0 determining when grouping pays. Single-agent probes recover the sign of δ \delta correctly in 81 % 81\% of cases, compared with 56 % 56\% for always grouping. The gap A ⁡ ( n , W ) − A ⁡ ( 1 , W ) A(n,W)-A(1,W) is interior in n n and collapses under tight windows across all five models (Appendix Figure 8 ), a generation-floor effect since raising g min g_{\min} recovers the worst cell (Appendix Figure 10 ). Directly measuring Δ ​ p max \Delta p_{\max} per agent at fixed g g , gives a small, sign-mixed estimate across four model-task cells (Appendix Table 15 ), so we find no reliable ceiling gain from reading a peer, consistent with debate’s apparent gains coming from the vote and not from Δ ​ p max \Delta p_{\max} . Further details are in Appendix D.2 . sections.heading: The reading cost m m .
sections.text: m m is the token cost of reading one peer message (Eq. 1 ), determining how quickly added agents reduce the group’s shared thinking room. Both the collapse and interior optimum arise from m > 0 m>0 . Setting m = 0 m{=}0 holds g g fixed regardless of group size, as in debate where each agent has its own window. The theory then predicts the largest feasible group at every window, with no interior optimum and no collapse (Appendix Figure 9 ). More details are in Appendix D.6 .

sections.heading: The price of a token.
sections.text: We ablate the output-to-input price ratio r = c out / c in r{=}c_{\text{out}}/c_{\text{in}} to reflect practical cost models, where reading and generating tokens can have different prices. Making input more expensive reduces their performance accordingly and TB-MAD keeps the lowest regret at every ratio tried on these spends (Appendix Table 19 ), while cheaper input buys a larger cost-optimal group at the same spend (Appendix Figure 6 ).

sections.heading: Is the collapse a long-context artifact?
sections.text: A longer transcript could hurt through position ( Liu et al., 2024a ; Hsieh et al., 2024 ) or length alone ( Levy et al., 2024 ) , but these effects do not explain the collapse. Moving the question to the end of the transcript, after the peer messages, at fixed H H and g g changes accuracy by less than 1 % 1\% on average (Appendix Table 23 ). Question position moves the collapse cell without lifting it out of collapse.

sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: We develop a token-budget theory of when additional context is worth its cost by placing reading and thinking in a shared window. The theory predicts optimal group size and identifies a critical window below which a single agent can outperform debate. Empirically, our method achieves the lowest regret under tight budgets, while self-consistency often matches or outperforms debate at lower cost. The theory offers a simple guide for when to read more, think more, or add agents. Limitations and Future work are discussed in Appendix E .

sections.heading: AI use statement
sections.text: In this work, we used generative AI tools solely to support writing, including proofing, language polishing, and improving readability. We did not use them to develop research ideas, conduct experiments, or generate the substantive content of the work. All AI-assisted text was reviewed and verified by the authors, who take full responsibility for the final content.

sections.heading: Ethics statement
sections.text: TB-MAD lowers the token cost of deploying multi-agent debate by choosing a group size before any debate is run. Its predictions are calibrated per model and task, so a size chosen outside the regime the probe sweep covers can lose accuracy with no signal that it has. We use only public benchmarks and open-weight models, with no human subjects or personal data.

sections.heading: Reproducibility statement
sections.text: All model equations, proofs and implementation details are in Appendices B and A.1 – A.3 . We will release the code, the banked debate transcripts and the table and figure generation scripts openly for research purposes upon publication.

sections.heading: D.2 Voting against talking, and the single agent
sections.text: Two secondary consequences follow from the same comparison: self-consistency weakly dominates debate (Prop. 2 ), and forming a group is not always worthwhile ( δ ≤ 0 \delta\leq 0 ).

sections.heading: Where the margin is largest, and how firmly.
sections.text: Prop. 2 implies that the self-consistency margin is set by the per-vote ability consumed by peer reading. It is therefore largest when the generation window binds and shrinks as the window loosens, eventually vanishing once both methods reach their best size at sufficiently large W W (Figures 4 – 5 ). The large gap at the tightest window is partly a clipping effect: many ( n , W = 1200 ) (n,W{=}1200) cells collapse to the same clipped generation room, whereas restricting to unclipped cells reduces the margin from + 42.0 +42.0 to + 13.7 % +13.7\% . A question-clustered paired bootstrap with 2000 2000 resamples confirms the cell-level effect; applying the same test per window gives the SC sig. W W column in Table 18 .

sections.heading: Where the closed form gets the sign wrong.
sections.text: CSQA is the one task where the closed form recovers the δ \delta sign poorly, most severely on Gemma3-12B (predicted 24 % 24\% , the lowest cell in Table 18 ). The per-cell fit there has k ≈ 8.6 k{\approx}8.6 , an unusually steep Hill curve, fit to only seven calibration points; its leave-one-out RMSE is over an order of magnitude above its in-sample RMSE, the signature of overfitting rather than of a genuine near-step response. Combined with c w c_{w} estimates that are the least stable of any task (Table 21 ), the fitted ϕ \phi crosses the break-even β \beta almost as soon as the window opens, so the closed form predicts the group winning at every swept size while the group in fact never does. All five models show the same direction of error on CSQA, so this is a property of the task’s fit stability, not an isolated bug in one cell.

sections.heading: Appendix E Limitations and Future work
sections.text: First , the aggregation model is a tractable approximation rather than an exact account of group behavior. It relies on equicorrelation, a fixed error concentration, and an unweighted, average-based decision threshold, all of which are empirically evaluated rather than assumed to hold exactly; consensus-weighted aggregation ( Nguyen et al., 2026a ) is not considered. Moreover, although we investigate heterogeneous model sets, allocation remains uniform across agent counts; adaptive allocation ( Nguyen et al., 2026b ) is an interesting direction for future work. Second , the analysis focuses on self-generated computation, including debate and self-refinement, and does not cover settings where additional context is retrieved or supplied externally, such as retrieval-augmented generation. Third , all five models have at most 12B parameters and short fitted solution lengths g 0 g_{0} , ranging from 137 137 to 478 478 tokens. Models with thousand-token reasoning chains would have much larger g 0 g_{0} , shifting the collapse regime to larger windows and potentially beyond deployed context lengths. We expect the qualitative shape to transfer, but not the specific operating points. Fourth , additional revision rounds increase visibility and may shift the trade-off if their revision benefit does not offset the added context cost; Appendix D.1 explores R R up to 3 for self-refinement. Fifth , the whole account assumes one window pays for reading and generation. Under per-agent contexts, reading does not consume generation room, m = 0 in our accounting, and the interior optimum disappears ( § \lx@sectionsign 4.3 ). A Token-Budget Theory of Reasoning with Shared Context Manh Nguyen † † thanks: Corresponding Author Sunil Gupta Hung Le Affiliation: Applied Artificial Intelligence Initiative, Deakin University, Australia Affiliation: {manh.nguyen, sunil.gupta, thai.le}@deakin.edu.au Abstract Reasoning systems increasingly improve answers by incorporating additional context into the model’s input, from multi-agent debate, where agents read their peers’ responses, to self-refinement, where a model revisits its own drafts. In these systems, communication consumes context as one agent’s output becomes another’s input. We study the regime where token reading and generation draw on one fixed token window, so every token spent reading is a token that cannot be spent reasoning. We develop a token-budget theory that formalizes this trade-off, modeling accuracy as a function of the reasoning budget remaining after reading and aggregating votes with a Condorcet jury model that permits correlated errors. For multi-agent debate, the theory gives a closed-form prediction for the optimal number of agents. This quantity is estimated from single-agent measurements, allowing the optimal group size to be determined without running debate, and the same accounting extends to a heterogeneous set of different models. We empirically verify our theory and show that, at the predicted group size, our method outperforms strong baselines under the tightest calibration spend, where debate-calibrated rules can afford only one or two questions. Self-refinement obeys the same accounting, with its own draft in place of a peer message. The theory further predicts that communication pays only when the gain in the accuracy ceiling exceeds the reasoning room spent on reading, with this condition tightening as the window shrinks. Across five open models and four reasoning tasks, self-consistency matches or beats deployed debate at 93 93 % of 980 980 matched window-and-group-size settings, with the gap being largest under tight windows and nearly disappearing at a loose one, consistent with the theory. Under a shared window, how much room a model has left to think matters more than what it reads . 1 Introduction Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in reasoning pipelines that reuse model-generated text as input to subsequent computation. Multi-agent debate exchanges answers among agents ( Du et al., 2024 ; Liang et al., 2024 ) , while self-refinement feeds a model its own previous drafts ( Madaan et al., 2023 ) . Such reuse can improve reasoning by providing additional information, but under a fixed token budget, it also raises a fundamental question: not whether added feedback helps, but how much it is worth in terms of the reasoning budget it consumes. Figure 1: Overview of our method (Qwen2.5-7B, GSM8K). One window W W pays for both reading (question plus peer messages) and thinking (generation g g ), and each extra agent adds m m tokens of reading. The per-agent edge δ \delta is the gap between the probability of the correct answer and that of the strongest wrong answer: larger δ \delta means a stronger correct-answer margin, while δ ≤ 0 \delta\leq 0 means that a wrong answer is at least as likely. Left : The dashed line marks the smallest thinking room at which δ > 0 \delta>0 ; a group that reads past it (here n = 8 n{=}8 ) leaves too few tokens for reasoning and its accuracy collapses. Right : The effective sample size n eff n_{\mathrm{eff}} measures the independent-vote equivalent of n n correlated agents, while δ \delta falls as thinking room shrinks. Their product S S , the synergy index, therefore captures the trade-off between per-agent accuracy and voting amplification and peaks at n ∗ = 4.9 n^{\ast}=4.9 . The shaded band marks δ ≤ 0 \delta{\leq}0 , where votes amplify a wrong majority and extra agents cannot help. Majority-voting analyses predict that adding agents amplifies a correct majority until correlated errors cap the gain ( Ladha, 1992 ; Liu et al., 2026 ) . However, on multi-hop reasoning tasks, a single long chain-of-thought ( Wei et al., 2022 ) often matches or outperforms a multi-agent system under an equal thinking budget ( Tran and Kiela, 2026 ) . Debate also does not consistently outperform self-consistency on an accuracy-per-token-cost frontier ( Smit et al., 2024 ; Bertalanic and Fortuna, 2026 ) , echoing the broader trade-off between token expenditure and accuracy in sampling and search ( Snell et al., 2025 ; Brown et al., 2024 ) . The token budget deserves separate attention because it corresponds directly to the cost incurred in practice. At current API prices, inference can range from cents to tens of dollars per million tokens, depending on the model and provider ( OpenAI, 2026 ; Google, 2026 ; Anthropic, 2026 ) . For multi-agent debate, the cost grows further with the number of agents n n (group size): adding agents increases not only the amount of reasoning generated, but also the amount of peer text that must be read and processed. Existing work attacks this cost either by compressing agent communication or by fixing the reasoning budget, but treats communication and reasoning as separate costs, despite both consuming the same token budget ( § \lx@sectionsign 2 ). Once the token budget is viewed this way, a trade-off appears: with n n small, more of the budget remains for thinking, while with n n large, most of it is spent on reading peer messages, leaving little room to reason. The question is then how to estimate the best group size n ∗ n^{\ast} for multi-agent debate under this trade-off. Existing approaches measure n n by sweeping or adaptively searching the design space, for instance, successive halving ( Jamieson and Talwalkar, 2016 ) . Both require debate runs to identify the operating point, without explaining why one group size is optimal or when adding more agents stops improving accuracy. We therefore introduce a token-budget theory that answers both questions in closed form. Consider homogeneous debate in which each agent, working under a window of W W tokens, must first pay for what it reads, namely the question and its peers’ messages, together H H tokens, plus a small fixed overhead c c . The remainder, g = W − H − c g=W-H-c , is the room it has left to reason. Instead of assigning each agent a fixed chance of voting correctly, we introduce its ability , which is the accuracy it reaches when its reasoning is capped at g g tokens. Ability grows with thinking room, too little room can prevent an agent from reaching an answer, while beyond a sufficient room, additional tokens yield little further gain. We let it grow with g g (Eq. 3 ) via the fittable thinking-gain function ϕ \phi , whose functional form and parameters can be calibrated from held-out calibration data. We then combine the resulting votes with a Condorcet jury model that allows correlated errors, developing the per-answer margin δ \delta (Eq. 6 ), the group accuracy A ⁡ ( n ) A(n) , the effective sample size n eff n_{\mathrm{eff}} and the synergy index S ⁡ ( n ) = δ ​ n eff S(n)=\delta\sqrt{n_{\mathrm{eff}}} (Eq. 10 ) in Section 3 . Figure 1 provides an overview of our method. Our model yields a closed-form prediction of an interior optimal group size n ∗ n^{\ast} that moves with the budget . It is read off single-agent measurements: we measure the ability curve with a cap sweep and estimate one error-correlation parameter at the initial round , then predict group size without running the debate. With a sufficiently large budget, our predictions approach the classical correlation-limited ensemble, where the main benefit comes from aggregating independent evidence. The practical advantage of our approach is therefore greatest in the tight-budget regime, where choosing the group size correctly matters most and our method achieves the best accuracy-budget trade-off. At the predicted size, it incurs only a 1.4 % 1.4\% accuracy gap from a per-cell oracle, using between 26 26 and 79 79 calibration questions depending on the cell, where the debate-calibrated rules use only one or two at matched spend. The accounting extends to a heterogeneous model set, where the rule chooses which models to include as well as how many. Our framework also clarifies the cost of communication relative to self-consistency ( Wang et al., 2023 ) . Self-consistency leaves the full window available for reasoning, whereas debate spends part of that budget processing peer responses, so communication must provide sufficient informational benefit to justify this cost. In our experiments, self-consistency matches or beats deployed debate at 93 % 93\% of the 980 980 matched operating points, while a paired test finds debate significantly ahead at only 0.5 % 0.5\% . The gap is largest under tight budgets and nearly disappears at a loose budget, where communication consumes a smaller share of the available reasoning budget. Self-refinement, which rereads only its own last draft without voting, pays the same fixed reading cost every round with none of the amplification that voting provides, so its accuracy collapses faster than debate’s as rounds accumulate. Our contributions are as follows. First , we introduce a token-budget theory that predicts the optimal debate size n ∗ n^{\ast} in closed form and extends to heterogeneous model sets, outperforming strong baselines under the tightest calibration spend without running a debate. Second , the theory reveals when debate’s voting benefits outweigh its communication cost relative to self-consistency under the same token budget. Third , ablations show that reading cost drives collapse and the interior optimum, with robustness tests covering longer reasoning and practical token pricing. 2 Related Work Multi-agent debate in LLMs. LLM instances critique and revise each other’s answers to improve reasoning relative to a single pass ( Du et al., 2024 ; Liang et al., 2024 ) , and voting over more agents can improve accuracy in practice ( Wang et al., 2023 ; Li et al., 2024a ) . Each additional agent, however, also introduces peer messages that other agents must process, increasing the communication burden of the group. Existing work addresses this burden by reducing communication through sparse speaker selection, group partitioning, or retaining only conflicting messages ( Li et al., 2024b ; Liu et al., 2024b ; Zeng et al., 2025 ; Nguyen et al., 2026c ) . A complementary line studies whether debate is worthwhile under a matched sampling or thinking budget, with several works finding that self-correction or a single long reasoning chain can match or outperform debate ( Huang et al., 2024 ; Tran and Kiela, 2026 ; Bertalanic and Fortuna, 2026 ) . A third line promotes diversity through heterogeneous model sets, arguing that homogeneous evaluation overvalues debate ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) , attributing vanilla debate’s weakness to lost candidate diversity ( Zhu et al., 2026 ) , and showing that mixed panels revise less harmfully than homogeneous ones ( Nilayam et al., 2026 ) . Beyond debate, this idea appears in mixtures of agents ( Wang et al., 2025 ) , model routing ( Ong et al., 2025 ) , and cost-aware cascades ( Chen et al., 2023 ) . Estimating the operating point. Existing approaches search the design space, e.g., via successive halving ( Jamieson and Talwalkar, 2016 ) , or learn the operating point from data, but both require debate runs for calibration. Chen et al. (2024) make voting accuracy non-monotone in call count through query-difficulty diversity, but their optimum is refit separately at each budget, whereas ours transfers from a single-agent cap sweep. Liu et al. (2026) give the closest theoretical treatment, deriving an amplification-collapse threshold in closed form from a power-law ability curve. Their ability curve is calibrated in simulation and remains concave, so it cannot capture the near-zero accuracy below the minimum length needed for a solution, the regime where our collapse occurs. Their accounting also holds the per-agent generation allowance fixed, so adding an agent costs no reasoning room, making their collapse a consequence of correlation alone rather than reading. We recover their setting as the m = 0 m=0 case ( § \lx@sectionsign 4.3 ). Token Budgeting in LLMs. A separate line studies how to allocate a fixed token budget across samples or reasoning length for a single agent, including token budgets for chain-of-thought, budget forcing at decoding time, budget-aligned tree search, and the non-monotone effect of reasoning length on task success ( Han et al., 2025 ; Muennighoff et al., 2025 ; Miyamoto et al., 2026 ; Qi, 2026 ) . Controlled comparisons at matched sampling or search budgets find that voting, rather than talking, carries the gain ( Choi et al., 2025 ; Kaesberg et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2024a ) , while Wunderlich et al. (2026) report the opposite ordering under per-agent rather than shared contexts. These methods budget within reasoning or sampling, leaving peer text outside the account. 3 Method We formalize the token-budget problem behind debate, define per-agent ability as a function of the room left to think, and turn it into a group-accuracy prediction. The theory predicts optimal group size and identifies a critical window below which a single agent can outperform debate. Empirically, our method achieves the lowest regret under tight budgets, while self-consistency often matches or outperforms debate at lower cost. The theory offers a simple guide for when to read more, think more, or add agents. Limitations and Future work are discussed in Appendix E .
